nm_little_horse_mesa.blurb: Little Horse Mesa is a short basalt cliff inside Sugarite Canyon State Park, up on the mesa edge above the creek valley near Raton. The walls stand roughly 40 to 50 feet and are split by vertical cracks, with some face climbing between them. It is almost entirely a gear-protected crag, and nearly every line can also be top-roped from the rim, which makes it handy for mixed parties. Most climbs fall between 5.8 and 5.10 with a handful of harder ones. The elevation keeps summer days comfortable, and the rock is generally sound. The walk to the base crosses brambles and talus, so expect a scrappy trail.
nm_little_horse_mesa.approach: Leave the road at the Little Horse Mesa trail signpost, take the right fork, and watch for a cairn on your left. A faint path then winds through brambles and talus down to the base. You arrive at the far left end of the cliff. Another option is to hike to the mesa top and come at the cliff from above, which suits the right-hand lines better.

nm_playground_the.blurb: The Playground is a south-facing basalt cliff of about 60 feet on the canyon rim at White Rock, near Los Alamos. It is the area's busiest top-rope crag, with crack and face lines that are mostly led on gear, and the base can also be bouldered. Grades cluster around 5.10 and 5.11, with a good number of 5.9s for easing in. Because it faces south it soaks up sun, which suits cool months and makes summer afternoons hot. The cliff sits in a residential neighborhood, so be considerate of the street and the houses on the way in.
nm_playground_the.parking_note: Pull up on the street near house number 719 on Meadow Lane, keeping clear of driveways and mailboxes.
nm_playground_the.approach: Take the public path squeezed between two houses, turn right at the rim, and walk about 300 yards. Look for the gully with a small basalt tower on its left; the cliff is at the bottom of that gully.

nm_dead_cholla_wall.blurb: Dead Cholla Wall is a basalt crag on the west rim of the Rio Grande Gorge above Taos, mixing sport lines with gear-protected cracks. The rock is hard and pocketed, with small in-cut holds on the faces and splitter cracks ranging from fingers to wider. Most climbs are 5.10 to 5.12, with 5.11 the largest group and a thin selection of easier ones. It faces east, so it gets strong early sun and fades into shade later in the day, which works well for hot afternoons and chilly mornings alike. Many routes have chains for rigging a top rope, and the walk from the trailhead is quick.
nm_dead_cholla_wall.approach: A short stroll of a few hundred yards from the trailhead brings you to the top of the crag. The trail starts at the parking area on the gorge rim.

nm_miner_s_crag.blurb: Miner's Crag sits on the west side of the Rio Grande Gorge north of John Dunn Bridge, a quiet, remote-feeling wall reached by dropping into the canyon. It offers a roughly even split between trad and sport, with short routes packed closely together. Expect crimps, flat edges and cracks on vertical to slightly overhanging rock; the cracks can be jagged or hollow, so gear placements take care. Grades spread across 5.8 to 5.11 with a few harder lines. Gorge walls generally catch winter morning sun and work well in the afternoon during warmer months. The descent trail is steep and loose in places.
nm_miner_s_crag.approach: From the Montoso road parking, walk back along a two-track and watch for cairns at the first rock outcrops. Follow them down a steep trail into the gorge, then traverse right along a loose shale path to the cliff base. Allow around twenty minutes in all.

nm_mosaic_rock.blurb: Mosaic Rock is the largest formation at Tres Piedras, a granite dome of around 200 feet standing in pine country west of Taos. The south face carries the longest and most numerous lines, while the north side has shorter routes that stay shady and are often breezy. Climbing is mostly trad on slab and face terrain where friction matters, with bolts few and far between and some runouts to respect. Grades run from the 5.7s through 5.12, with the bulk between 5.8 and 5.11. The walk in passes South Rock, and the descent is an easy downclimb down a gully on the east end.

nm_big_cat_canyon_a_k_a_spider_canyon.blurb: Big Cat Canyon, also called Spider Canyon, is a small bouldering canyon in the Ponderosa area of the Jemez, around 7,700 feet. Boulders stand on both sides in a spot sheltered from wind and shaded by ponderosa pines for much of the day. The volcanic tuff is grainy and pocketed where the patina is thin, but it is new, coarse rock where holds can snap and skin takes a beating. Problems run from VB to V7, with V2 to V3 the most common and a cluster of V6s for the strong. Bring several pads: some landings are flat but others sit on steep hillside.

nm_south_east_side.blurb: This is the southeast-facing side of The Overlook, White Rock's best-known crag, a basalt cliff on the canyon rim above the Rio Grande. A roughly even split between sport and gear routes, nearly all with bolted anchors, with some lines also set up for top-roping from the rim. Grades are mostly 5.9 to 5.11 with a few 5.12s. Because the other side of the crag faces northwest, the Overlook can be climbed in many seasons, and this southeast side is especially pleasant on warm winter days. The rock can be fragile in places, so a helmet is wise.
nm_south_east_side.parking_note: Drive to the end of the Overlook Park road and park by the roundabout near the viewpoint.

nm_a1_utopian_vista_upper_tier.blurb: The Upper Tier is the higher wall at Utopian Vistas, on the Rio Grande Gorge rim above Taos. The rock is dark, hard, pocketed basalt, and the climbing ranges from vertical faces to overhanging jug hauls, with technical corners, roofs and thin cracks. Sport and gear-protected routes are mixed, and the mid-range is strong: 5.10 and especially 5.11 dominate. The terrain is relatively new, so loose holds are possible and a helmet makes sense. Gorge walls tend to face east, giving sun on winter mornings and workable afternoons during warmer months.
nm_a1_utopian_vista_upper_tier.approach: Leave from the Dead Cholla trailhead lot and follow the West Rim Trail for roughly a quarter hour. When you reach the rim of a wash, head down toward the edge and follow cairns north along the foot of the wall.

nm_below_the_old_new_place.blurb: Below The Old New Place is a basalt cliff of about 60 feet one level beneath the Old New Place on the White Rock canyon rim. It is one of the town's top sport spots and holds the area's densest group of hard routes, with 5.11 and 5.12 making up most of what is here, along with some gear lines and a few easier warm-ups. The edge above is loose and sloping with little to anchor to, so it suits leading better than top-roping. The rock is basalt that can be brittle, so helmets help. Reaching it means dropping two tiers down the rim.
nm_below_the_old_new_place.parking_note: Park on Meadow Lane close to house number 719, leaving driveways and mailboxes clear.
nm_below_the_old_new_place.approach: Use the public path between two houses and walk out to the rim. Work down two levels into the canyon, passing the base of the Old New Place, and carry on to the next level, bearing slightly right.

nm_potrillo_cliffs.blurb: Potrillo Cliffs is a short basalt cliff on the White Rock rim, about 45 feet high and bent into an L shape, with one face looking south and another west. It is the town's favored beginner crag, mostly trad and top-rope with good protection and plenty of climbs in the 5.6 to 5.10 range, so it can fill up. A few harder lines reach into the 5.12 range. Some routes have bolted anchors, but carrying trad gear or slinging trees is the safer plan. The base is reached by a third-class scramble down the east side, which can be awkward for small children or dogs.
nm_potrillo_cliffs.approach: Follow the trail from the street out to a large gate and sign, go a short way beyond, and bear left to the cliff top. A third-class scramble down the east side lands you at the base, about ten minutes in total.
